name: Front Headlock System
description: The front headlock system chains snapdown into guillotine, D'Arce, anaconda, or go-behind as a continuous attack sequence. It is the most powerful upper-body control system in no-gi grappling.
shortInstruction: From head control, chain attacks in this order: snapdown → guillotine → D'Arce → anaconda → go-behind. Keep your head on the outside and never give up the front headlock position.
summary: The front headlock system is a continuous attack sequence from the front headlock position (one arm around the head, the other controlling the far arm or hip). From this position, you cycle through submissions and positional advances: the snapdown breaks their posture, the guillotine threatens the neck, the D'Arce attacks the neck from the side, the anaconda attacks from the front, and the go-behind takes the back. The key is to never give up the front headlock — if one attack fails, immediately transition to the next.
whyItWorks: The front headlock position controls the opponent's head and one arm — the two primary tools for balance and defense
Chaining five attacks from one position creates an unsolvable dilemma — they cannot defend all five
The front headlock is available from sprawls, snapdowns, and failed takedowns — it is the most common scramble position
Each attack in the chain sets up the next: the guillotine threat opens the D'Arce, the D'Arce opens the go-behind
commonMistakes: Giving up the front headlock to reset — once you have the position, chain attacks rather than resetting
Committing too fully to one submission — the chain requires 70% commitment, 30% awareness to transition
Letting the opponent sit up or re-establish base — maintain head pressure throughout
Not protecting your own position — keep your head on the outside and your hips low
coachingCues: Never give up the front headlock
safetySummary: The D'Arce and anaconda chokes can come on fast — apply controlled pressure and release on tap
Do not crank the neck during the snapdown — the snapdown controls posture, it does not attack the neck
If the opponent rolls out of the front headlock, protect your head and re-establish control before continuing the chain
keyCorrections: If the opponent keeps escaping the chain: you are giving up the head position — maintain head pressure between attacks
If you cannot lock the D'Arce: the arm is not deep enough — walk your hand deeper into their armpit before locking
If they take your back: you let your head drift inside — keep your head on the outside throughout

systemLogic.corePrinciple: The front headlock system has five attacks in a specific sequence: Snapdown → Guillotine → D'Arce → Anaconda → Go-Behind

decisionTree.action: snap the opponent's head to the mat, breaking their posture. This is the entry to all subsequent attacks
as their head drops, slide your choking arm under their chin and lock the guillotine. If they defend, transition to D'Arce
when they defend the guillotine by pulling their head back, feed your choking arm deeper into their far armpit and lock the D'Arce by connecting your hands. The D'Arce attacks the neck from the side
if the D'Arce fails (they turn into you), switch the lock to the other side and apply the anaconda. The anaconda attacks the neck from the front
if all chokes fail, release the head and circle behind them to take the back. The front headlock position naturally transitions to a back take

moneyDetails: The front headlock system is the most important upper-body attack system in no-gi — it is used at every level of grappling
Mastering the front headlock chain gives you five attacks from one position — you almost always finish
The front headlock is the primary scoring position from sprawls and snapdowns — it is the most common wrestling exchange
fixItFast: If you cannot lock any choke: go straight to the go-behind — the front headlock always has the back take option
If the opponent pulls their arms free: reset the front headlock with a tighter head grip
If they sit up: drive them back down with the snapdown before starting the chain
